newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU plans major BSE research amid new fears.
newsitem.headline: EU plans major BSE research amid new fears.

text.p: The European Commission said on Wednesday it would fund major research into diseases like BSE, as scientists warned deaths from its human equivalent could rise sharply from transfusions of contaminated blood.
"The European people would like to know, quite legitimately, the scale of the risk arising from animal diseases," Research Commissioner Edith Cresson told a news conference.

Fifteen million Ecus ($19 million) are available now for research into bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) or mad cow disease, its human version Creutzfeld-Jakob Disease (CJD), and scrapie, a similar disease found in sheep.
European Union research ministers will consider on December 3 whether to let the Commission spend a further 35 million Ecus.
The research will try to discover the origin of prion diseases like BSE, how they are transmitted to humans, a reliable live diagnostic test and ways of treating those affected.
"These matters are urgent," European Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler tolds reporters a day after the alarm was sounded by Eric Postaire, a former director of the Paris hospitals pharmacy.

The reaction to BSE and CJD was reminiscent of the early eighties, when most people rejected the idea that AIDS was caused by a virus, he told the European Parliament's committee of inquiry into the BSE crisis.
He said that while lack of experience in the 1980s might be an excuse for not acting more swiftly to prevent an epidemic, that was not the case now.
Postaire said he feared cases of CJD would rise dramatically because of the risk of infection through blood transfusions.
"CJD has a five- to 10-year incubation period," he said.
"Blood transfusions are an excellent way of transmitting it from one person to another because, unlike cases of the HIV virus or hepatitis C, we can only do post-mortem tests for CJD."
Postaire warned there could be more, even less obvious sources of infection, such as anti-wrinkle creams containing collagen from cattle.
As collagen creams are no longer classed as pharmaceutical products in Europe, their use is not controlled by government health authorities, he said.
Commissioner Cresson urged EU governments to release the money for the research which they failed to do in October.
"The public would find it difficult to understand that the EU is spending a considerable amount to compensate farmers in difficulty but is being miserly over research," she said.
The EU has committed 1.35 billion in aid to beef producers since the BSE crisis broke in March. ($1= 0.79 Ecu)
